content: Chromophobia, also referred to as chromatophobia or chrematophobia, is a persistent and irrational fear or aversion to colors. This condition is typically a learned or conditioned response. Although clinical phobias specifically related to colors are rare, colors can provoke hormonal responses and psychological reactions in individuals. The term chromophobia can also describe an aversion to the use of color in products or design. In cellular biology, chromophobe or chromophobic cells are a classification of cells that do not attract hematoxylin, a staining agent, and this is associated with a process known as chromatolysis. There are specific terms for the fear of particular colors, such as erythrophobia for the fear of red and leukophobia for the fear of white. A fear of the color red is often linked to a fear of blood. In his 2000 book Chromophobia, artist and writer David Batchelor discusses how Western culture has historically treated color as corrupting, foreign, or superficial. Anthropologist Michael Taussig suggests that cultural aversion to color can be traced back over a thousand years, with Batchelor attributing its origins to Aristotle’s preference for line over color in art and philosophy. In a study, hatchling loggerhead sea turtles were observed to have an aversion to lights in the yellow wavelength spectrum. This behavior is thought to help them orient themselves toward the ocean. Similarly, the Mediterranean sand smelt (Atherina hepsetus) has shown an aversion to red objects placed near its tank, while it investigates objects of other colors. In other experiments, geese have been conditioned to develop adverse reactions to foods of a specific color, although this reaction was not observed when they were exposed to colored water. In Alfred Hitchcock’s film Marnie, the title character exhibits an aversion to the color red, which stems from a traumatic event in her childhood. Hitchcock conveys this aversion using expressionistic techniques, such as overlaying a wash of red over close-up shots of Marnie to visually represent her psychological distress.
